title: Theodore Roosevelt didn't create the NCAA; a campus death did
dek: After 1905's ‘death harvest’, the NCAA's rules committee came from the NYU president bypassing the Big Three, not from Roosevelt's conference.
why: One core reversal: the NCAA's true architect wasn't Theodore Roosevelt but an inter-university power struggle.
who: Founders and investors interested in college sports history and NCAA governance, plus anyone curious how regulatory bodies emerge from crisis.

points.h: The flying wedge transplanted military tactics directly to the field
points.body: Without forward-pass rules, 1870s football became pure collision. Offenses formed a V-shaped flying wedge—one player at the point, teammates behind using collective force to drive him forward. The tactic borrowed its name directly from military wedge-charge formations. Head protection was minimal—just long hair and a wool cap. Defense meant launching another group of bodies into collision.

points.h: Football became combat training to preserve young men's military fitness
points.body: After the Civil War, America's economy shifted from agriculture to commerce, raising fears that young men would lose combat readiness. Football filled the void: it demanded obedience, teamwork, strength, and courage—military virtues. The sport's violence wasn't accidental; society actively encouraged it.

points.h: Nineteen players died in 1905, defining college football's deadliest year
points.body: In 1905, roughly 19 people died in college football games—including high schoolers and amateurs, not just college players—while 137 suffered serious injuries. The San Francisco Call documented the causes: 4 deaths from internal collision injuries, 6 from concussions, 3 from spinal damage, plus 19 skull fractures. This toll drove every subsequent reform.

points.h: Theodore Roosevelt's White House summit produced no rule changes
points.body: Roosevelt, a football enthusiast whose son was injured in 1905, brought Harvard, Princeton, and Yale presidents to the White House to demand safer play. Historian Eric Moyen called it a ‘nothing burger’: the three dominant programs had no incentive to change rules that would help rivals compete. A month passed with no action.

points.h: The real reform catalyst was a player's death at Thanksgiving
points.body: A player's death at Thanksgiving 1905 in an NYU-Union College game pushed NYU's president to act. He sent a telegram to Harvard's president demanding a new meeting; when refused, he bypassed the Big Three, convened every college president with a football team, and they established the rules committee that became the NCAA.

points.h: Forward-pass legalization was designed to break up mass collisions
points.body: The committee swiftly changed the rules: first-down advancement moved from 5 to 10 yards, and the forward pass became legal in 1906. The goal was clear—disperse players across the field to catch passes instead of forming solid lines for head-on collision. This was the crisis's most direct technical legacy.

points.h: The NCAA fought over money and power from its founding
points.body: Despite the safety crisis driving its creation, the committee was ‘never just about safety’, according to historian Eric Moyen. It debated payment for players, their name-and-image rights (the precursor to NIL), academic standards for athletes, and—most crucially—who enforces the rules: the NCAA, individual universities, or coaches. These exact issues resurfaced virtually unchanged a century later.

points.h: Today's NIL chaos echoes the 1905 power vacuum exactly
points.body: The confusion around NIL, transfer portals, and coaching salaries directly mirrors 1905, according to Moyen: then, university presidents negotiated safety rules among themselves; now, leagues and coaches must negotiate money and authority instead. Same power vacuum, different stakes. The NCAA declined to comment. No clear answer exists yet.
